title: Intention is the act
hookLine: the Buddha calls intention itself kamma (AN 6.63)

lines: A LURCH, OR A LOOK FIRST.
cards: Two people step on your foot on the same crowded train. One lurches when the brakes hit. The other looks right at you first, and then does it.
Same foot. Same weight. Same bruise.
And yet nobody would call them the same event. No philosophy class required; a small child on a playground already argues the difference between an accident and on purpose.
The Buddha built a teaching on that instinct, and he put it in a single short sentence.

teach.b: The sentence is in the Numbered Discourses, in a sutta about seeing deeply into the teaching. The Buddha says, in plain terms: it is intention, monks, that I call kamma.
Having intended, a person acts by body, by speech, and by mind. The Pali word for intention is cetanā: the mind's leaning toward something, its choosing.
And kamma, karma in Sanskrit, simply means action, deed. Not fate. Not a cosmic scoreboard.
A deed. So this is a definition, and a startling one. Which part of the train was the deed?
Not the foot. The choosing. That's why the path spent days on right intention before it reached speech and action.

teach.h: THE MIND IS WHERE IT'S MADE.
teach.b: The hand and the tongue are where an act shows up; the mind is where it's made. Two things follow. First, accidents aren't the heart of kamma.
The lurch on the train isn't what the Buddha is pointing at, though carelessness can be a kind of choice too. Second, and harder: a deed can be done entirely inside.
A long, deliberate grudge is a deed, even if no one ever sees it. The Dhammapada opens with the same idea, in Max Müller's words: "All that we are is the result of what we have thought."
So if intention is the act, the place to practice is the half-second before the act.
That small gap is where the choosing lives, and the choosing is the part that's yours.

how: Buddhist teachers often explain kamma by pointing to intention, and many practitioners make a habit of checking their motive before acting and of dedicating good deeds with a wholesome wish.

o: fate, what's written for you at birth
action, a deed, made by intention
a cosmic score of rewards and punishments

games.q: what's inside kamma: tap the pairs.
p: intention is what I call kamma

s: kamma means action or deed; the Buddha defines it by intention.
in AN 6.63, a deed can be done by the mind alone
having intended, one acts by body, speech or mind.
by this definition, an accident weighs the same as deliberate harm
the choosing is the deed, though carelessness can be a kind of choice too.

games.q: two people step on your foot. one lurches when the brakes hit; one looks at you first. by AN 6.63, which is kamma in the full sense?
games.why: the Buddha calls intention kamma: the deed is the choosing, and the foot is only where it shows up.

practice: Rest with the breath and watch for the choosing: small impulses will arrive, to shift your weight, to scratch, to open your eyes, to check the time.
Before you act on one, see whether you can catch the intention itself, the little lean toward doing. You may act on it or not; the point is to see it before the body moves.

wordCard.voice: Kamma. Action, deed; karma in Sanskrit. The Buddha defines it by intention, cetanā: having intended, one acts.

orig.note: Pali kamma (Sanskrit karma, कर्म): action, deed. AN 6.63 defines it as intention.

carryVoice: Your line: the half-second before the act. The hand is where it shows; the mind is where it's made. Catch you tomorrow.

sources.work: The Dhammapada (Sacred Books of the East, vol. 10)
sources.q: All that we are is the result of what we have thought
